project_scope.note: Family reference began with exact-labeled Galphimia angustifolia video material; the current manifest also includes four canonical Malpighiaceae species. Species installation does not certify local nativity or fully verified photo anatomy.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: examine a complete opposite leaf, then one flower's five free petals and narrowed claws (petal stalks). When visible, check separate sepals, sepal glands, two-armed hairs and reproductive structures. Do not require sepal oil glands or a winged fruit for every genus.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Leaves are commonly simple and opposite, often with stipules. Many family members have characteristic two-armed or T-shaped hairs that are best treated as a magnified supporting character.
family_diagnostics.flower: Typically 5 free sepals and 5 free petals; petals are commonly clawed. Flowers often have 10 stamens and a superior, usually 3-carpellate ovary.
family_diagnostics.glands: New World Malpighiaceae often bear oil-secreting glands on the outer sepal surfaces, but glands may be reduced or absent in some lineages and should not be required.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Fruit architecture is diverse; splitting fruits and winged units occur in many genera.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: For a quick family hypothesis, pair opposite leaves with the peculiar free clawed petals; then use hairs, sepal glands and reproductive details as tie-breakers.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole flower → petal claw → sepal underside → reproductive/fruit confirmation
visual_lesson.intro: This family becomes much easier once you stop looking only at yellow petals and start looking at how each petal attaches.

steps.title: 1 · Start with the five free petals
steps.photo_role: Galphimia angustifolia flower / source-labeled family reference
steps.look_for: Five separate petals rather than a fused corolla tube.
steps.why_it_matters: This gives the learner the basic floral layout before zooming into the family-specific petal base.

steps.title: 2 · Follow a petal to its base
steps.look_for: A conspicuously narrowed, claw-like petal base leading into the broader blade.
steps.why_it_matters: The clawed petal is a high-value visual cue in the family and is clearly exposed by the current video frame.

steps.title: 3 · Flip the flower over
steps.look_for: Inspect the back of the sepals for paired or conspicuous glands rather than assuming they are present.
steps.why_it_matters: Oil glands are famous in New World Malpighiaceae but variable enough that they should confirm, not veto, an ID.

steps.title: 4 · Add the hair and fruit characters
steps.look_for: Under magnification, look for two-armed hairs; when fruit is present, inspect how the three-carpellate ovary matures and separates.
steps.why_it_matters: These characters prevent overfitting the family to one yellow-flowered Galphimia.

comparisons.title: Malpighiaceae vs Rosaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can show five free petals, but local-looking Rosaceae commonly use alternate leaves, a hypanthium and often numerous stamens; Malpighiaceae commonly uses opposite leaves, clawed petals and distinctive two-armed hairs.

comparisons.title: Do not require sepal oil glands
comparisons.rule: Oil glands are extremely useful when visible, but their reduction or absence in some Malpighiaceae means they are a confirmation character rather than a universal gate.

comparisons.title: Malpighiaceae versus Zygophyllaceae (Galphimia versus Kallstroemia)
comparisons.rule: Both can have opposite foliage and five showy petals. Galphimia angustifolia leaves are simple (one blade per petiole); Kallstroemia leaves are pinnately compound (paired leaflets on a shared axis). Check the entire leaf, mature fruit and petal base; flower color alone is not reliable. Kallstroemia often has about ten separate one-seeded mericarps.

comparisons.title: Malpighiaceae versus Polygalaceae (Galphimia versus Senega/Rhinotropis)
comparisons.rule: Galphimia's showy free organs are five petals with narrowed claws and generally ten stamens. Milkworts have two petal-like inner sepals (wings), a true lower keel petal and usually eight basally joined stamens. Confirm organ insertion on a real flower, not flower color or silhouette.

visual_lesson.caveat: The module now references four installed learner taxa; local nativity certification remains deferred. Some Malpighiaceae lack sepal oil glands; Cottsia bears dry winged units while Malpighia has fleshy fruit. No new photo is installed or visually certified by these anatomy requests.

anatomy_examples.plain_label: Narrow stalk at the base of a petal
anatomy_examples.look_for: An oblique close-up showing one of five free petals with its narrowed claw and broader blade. Include a whole flower for context.
anatomy_examples.photo_role: exact-species oblique flower and petal-base macro
anatomy_examples.caption: Follow a free petal into its narrow claw; five free petals by themselves are not enough.

anatomy_examples.plain_label: Twining stem, tiny leaf hairs and dry winged fruit
anatomy_examples.botanical_label: twining habit, medifixed trichomes, winged mericarps
anatomy_examples.look_for: Matched stem/leaf context, true two-armed hair macro when visible, and mature dry winged fruit; record the historical name Janusia gracilis without replacing current Cottsia gracilis.
anatomy_examples.photo_role: exact-species whole vine, leaf-hair microdetail and mature winged-mericarps macro
anatomy_examples.caption: Winged fruit occurs in this vine but is not universal for the family.

anatomy_examples.plain_label: Small glands on sepals and fleshy ripe fruit
anatomy_examples.look_for: Show underside of flower with actual gland positions where present, plus unmistakable mature fleshy fruit. Avoid inferring unseen glands from the family name.
anatomy_examples.photo_role: exact-species sepal-underside macro and mature drupe photograph
anatomy_examples.caption: Compare gland-bearing sepals, when visible, with the fleshy fruit; not all Malpighiaceae form winged fruits.
